name: Stenstrom otoplasty

card.summary: An ear-pinning surgery that scores the front of the ear cartilage so it folds back into a natural antihelix, bringing prominent ears closer to the head for a more balanced profile.
card.note: Surgery under a plastic surgeon; complications such as hematoma, infection and overcorrection are described in the literature.

quick.overview:
Stenstrom otoplasty is a surgical technique for prominent (protruding) ears. The surgeon roughens or scores the front surface of the cartilage at the antihelical fold so the cartilage bends back on its own, creating the missing fold and setting the ear closer to the head.

People look to it for a more proportionate ear and a cleaner face and hair profile. It is described in the plastic surgery literature from the 1960s and 1970s, with later case series and technical refinements.
quick.how: The procedure is performed by a surgeon, usually on the ear cartilage through a small incision, sometimes with added steps such as reducing an enlarged concha or anchoring it with sutures. Adults often have local anesthesia with sedation and children general anesthesia; a head dressing and snug headband are typically worn afterward for weeks.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection that leaves unnatural contours. Choice of technique and surgeon varies, and published series are generally small and surgeon-reported.

lead: The Stenstrom otoplasty is an ear-pinning technique in which the surgeon scores or roughens the front of the antihelical cartilage so it bends away from the roughened side and forms a fold, without cutting through the cartilage [1][2]. It is used for prominent ears, whose causes include a missing antihelical fold, an open cephalo-conchal angle and an oversized concha [3][4].

People pursue it to bring protruding ears flat to the head and give a more balanced face outline, particularly because prominent ears can carry a psychological burden, especially in children facing teasing [3]. Within looksmaxxing-oriented lists of procedures, it appears among the named otoplasty methods.

Stenstrom's technique was published in 1963 and is one of several approaches alongside Mustarde mattress sutures, Furnas concha-mastoid sutures and Converse cartilage reshaping [1]. It is described as widely performed in France, and surgeons have published refinements such as an anterior rasp approach hidden under the upper helix and concha resection when needed [5].

angle.text: The surgery reshapes ear cartilage so a missing fold is created, pinning prominent ears closer to the head. The result is a more proportionate ear silhouette.

infobox: Absent antihelical fold, conchal hypertrophy, obtuse conchoscaphal angle [4]
General for children; local with sedation common in adults [1]

paras: In the original natural technique, the front surface of the cartilage at the antihelix is abraded or scored. Following the Gibson principle, cartilage tends to curve away from the roughened side toward the intact perichondrium, forming the fold [1]. A 2016 technical note describes modifications: introducing the rasp through an anterior approach hidden under the upper helical plication, removing part of the concha by a posterior approach in conchal hypertrophy, and burying the concha by suturing to mastoid periosteum after posterior auricular muscle resection [5]. The authors say the suture-less fold gives a natural look [5].
A 2024 Saudi case series evaluated a modified Stenstrom technique in six patients (12 ears) over one year of follow-up, and reported no complications [4].

Operating time ranges from about 1.5 to 5 hours and a dressing is worn for several days, followed by a snug headband for roughly 3 to 6 weeks, mostly at night [1]. Described complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection, the last being noted as the most significant [1].

An Italian clinical report from 1993 stated that Stenstrom otoplasty and/or concha-to-mastoid suturing was effective in 95% of its patients, with few complications [6]. A review of otoplasty states that each surgeon adopts a preferred technique to get a harmonious, durable result while avoiding complications such as infection [3].

Published reports are mainly surgeon-reported case series and technique descriptions, including a 1978 overview of the technique [2], a 1993 report [6], a 2016 refinement note [5] and a 2024 case series of six patients [4].
